summary.intent: Cut over-engineering from the Callisto release tooling: get an honest audit of where the assistant had added complexity without real value, then simplify the parts the user agreed were overkill, starting with the in-place JSON scanner.
summary.outcome: The user agreed the in-place JSON scanner was overkill, kept the weekly fuzz/mutation workflow and the per-crate coverage gate, and the assistant replaced the custom scanner with the maintained jsonc-parser (CST) crate. The 256 manifests tests and cargo deny passed, full CI was run, and a simplification PR was shipped. Earlier, PR #391 was opened with only a tap-notification step, a policy change and an AGENTS.md clause.

repo: Callisto version bumps in package.json are meant to produce a one-line diff; layout tests in callisto-manifests pin this behavior.
The workspace uses cargo deny for dependency checks, and new dependencies are declared in the root Cargo.toml then referenced from crate Cargo.tomls.

The release recovery queue (#383) can re-select a failed item on every push and has no lock, so it can wedge future releases. Manual dispatch with a full SHA already exists as a simpler recovery path.
The tap polls daily, which covers a missed post-release notification and makes extra checks on that notification unnecessary.
Work is done in git worktrees under .claude/worktrees (e.g. smoke-main).
In #365, batched git history cut process count from 78 to 33 but barely moved wall time because `cargo info` dominates; the parallel registry lookups in #364 had already captured the win.

code.finding: Rewritten to wrap the jsonc-parser CST (MIT, from dprint) for in-place JSON value edits instead of a hand-built scanner and diff layer.
Switched to the library-backed json_text edit path; the existing layout tests still pass.

workflow: Before writing any test, check or script, state the failure it prevents and how likely and costly it is. This was saved to memory by extending an existing entry.
When replacing bespoke code, check that a maintained library exists and fits (license, API surface) before building, then verify with existing tests, cargo deny and full CI.
Property tests and custom scanners are often overkill when a few unit tests or a library cover the need.
The user prefers fast, simple, straightforward solutions that add real value, and will override the assistant's proposed cuts selectively.

friction: The assistant over-built several pieces (JSON scanner with property test, batched git history, add-wizard prompter refactor), which prompted the user's pushback.
The custom JSON formatter in the property test needed a fixture patch from Codex, adding extra churn.
The blocking per-crate coverage gate was added after the user said meaningful tests matter more than the number, though the user later decided to keep it.
open_items: The 0.15.0 recovery is waiting on the user's go-ahead; the assistant recommends merging #391 first so the recovery is the first live test of the tap notification.
Decide whether to simplify or remove the release recovery queue (#383) in favor of documented manual recovery; the user has not decided.
Review the core release machinery (decision, intent, envelope, capability, observe/adopt/confirm) for over-complexity; this needs a deliberate decision.
Possible cuts not yet decided: `features-boundary` check, `add` wizard prompter refactor (#373), `init` message and `callisto.toml` root marker (#363), and the batched git history (#365).

Most of the ten proposed queue negative tests are probably to be dropped; one test, that a failed oldest item doesn't block later ones, is to be checked and written only if that is the actual behavior.
The in-progress lock for the queue is on hold until a duplicate run causes real harm.
